comments.author: shortrounddev2
comments.story: You Only Need a Tablet for Computer Science
comments.why: Introduces GDB and its TUI mode
comments.text: "You only need a tablet" (and remote infrastructure for actually writing your code on since a tablet won't work for 99% of assignments) I did the same thing in college, but with a Chromebook. I rented a VPS from Vultr and ssh'd in to write C and Java assignments with vim. VPS was $5/mo. Chromebooks can still write javascript code and run via the web browser, and you can actually mount a remote drive on a Chromebook (I think via sshfs?). From there you can use an electron based text editor like Atom (and I guess VSCode would work these days) and just compile and run programs via some SSH commands. I'll say anybody who wants to do the same thing with C should definitely check out GDB and its TUI mode: [VIDEO] But I think these days, running a GUI application over a network has become trivial. Back then, I don't remember any providers making it simple to deploy such projects

comments.author: daniel-levin
comments.story: Ask HN: What is the best practice for reading large pieces of C code?
comments.why: Intro to using gdb for reading large C codebases
comments.text: Compile it with debugging symbols and run it with gdb in tui mode. This will let you place breakpoints in source files, view back traces, find the definitions of functions, structures, macros, etc. The learning curve is a tad steep, but this video is pretty good: [VIDEO]
